question: A patient’s lymph node biopsy shows resting B cells clustered in a cortical region without germinal centers. Which anatomical site most likely contains these resting B cells?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the phases of the humoral immune response and where each of these occurring and which cell types are involved.

options.text: Primary follicle in lymph node cortex containing resting B cells
options.rationale: Correct: Primary follicles in the cortex house resting B cells before antigen encounter; this matches the lecture description of follicle anatomy.

options.text: Paracortex region of lymph node dominated by T cell zones
options.rationale: Wrong: Paracortex is T cell rich; it would be correct only if the question asked about activated T lymphocytes rather than resting B cells.

options.text: Medullary cords containing plasma cells and macrophage aggregates
options.rationale: Wrong: Medullary cords contain plasma cells and macrophages; this would be correct only if the sample showed antibody-secreting cells rather than resting B cells.

options.text: Marginal zone at splenic white pulp border with innate B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Marginal zone is a splenic structure with marginal-zone B cells; it would be correct only for spleen tissue rather than a lymph node cortex.

options.text: Germinal center within secondary follicle showing proliferating B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Germinal centers indicate active B cell proliferation and specialization; this would be correct only if the biopsy showed an active humoral response rather than resting follicles.

question: Which B cell subset can mount an antibody response to repetitive carbohydrate antigens without requiring helper lymphocyte signals?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast T-dependent vs. T-independent antibody responses and the different subsets of B cells.

options.text: Marginal-zone B cells respond to repetitive nonprotein antigens independently
options.rationale: Correct: Marginal-zone B cells respond to repetitive carbohydrate or lipid antigens without T cell help, as described for T-independent responses.

options.text: Follicular B cells require peptide antigen presentation and T cell help
options.rationale: Wrong: Follicular B cells are T-dependent responders; this would be correct only if the antigen were protein and required Tfh assistance.

options.text: B-1 cells are restricted to thymus-dependent protein antigen responses
options.rationale: Wrong: B-1 cells actually produce natural antibodies and can respond to nonprotein antigens; this option would be correct only if B-1 cells were limited to T-dependent responses.

options.text: Plasma cells immediately secrete high affinity class-switched antibodies
options.rationale: Wrong: Plasma cells secrete antibodies but high-affinity class-switched antibodies typically arise after T-dependent germinal center reactions; this would be correct only post affinity maturation.

options.text: Naïve B cells in bone marrow mediate rapid T-independent responses
options.rationale: Wrong: Naïve bone marrow B cells are not the primary mediators of peripheral T-independent responses; this would be correct only if those cells trafficked and functioned like marginal-zone or B-1 cells.

question: An experimental mouse lacks CD40L expression on CD4 cells. Which humoral process will be most impaired in this animal?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how CD4 T cells "help" B cells. Identify the predominant Th subset involved in the humoral response.

options.text: Isotype switching from IgM to IgG IgA or IgE will be impaired
options.rationale: Correct: CD40:CD40L interaction is required to activate AID and drive class switch recombination, so absence of CD40L blocks isotype switching.

options.text: Initial BCR cross-linking and naive B cell antigen recognition will be impaired
options.rationale: Wrong: BCR-mediated antigen recognition and cross-linking are independent of T cell CD40L; this would be correct only if BCR signaling molecules were absent.

options.text: Complement classical pathway activation by antibody complexes will be absent
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement activation depends on antibody isotypes like IgM and IgG binding antigen; it would be absent only if antibodies were not produced at all, not solely due to CD40L deficiency.

options.text: Follicular dendritic cell antigen display to B cells will be abolished
options.rationale: Wrong: FDC antigen display is independent of CD40L; this option would be correct only if FDCs were depleted or unable to bind antigen.

options.text: Somatic hypermutation in variable regions will be completely prevented
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation requires AID activation via T cell help; while CD40L deficiency reduces this process, it may not completely prevent all mutation without additional defects.

question: Which molecular event directly relocates the VDJ exon to a downstream constant region during antibody specialization?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: ii. Isotype Switching

options.text: Switch recombination excises intervening DNA between switch regions
options.rationale: Correct: Class switch recombination removes DNA between switch regions, moving the VDJ cassette adjacent to a new constant region as described in the lecture.

options.text: Somatic hypermutation introduces point mutations into constant region exons
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation targets variable regions, not constant regions; this would be correct only if mutations altered Fc function directly.

options.text: V(D)J recombination reorders constant region genes during activation
options.rationale: Wrong: V(D)J recombination assembles variable region exons during B cell development, not constant region switching; it would be correct only in early B cell maturation context.

options.text: Class switching copies constant region from helper T cell genome
options.rationale: Wrong: Class switching is an intrachromosomal recombination event within the B cell; this option would be correct only if horizontal gene transfer occurred, which it does not.

options.text: Alternative splicing of heavy chain transcripts changes Fc region identity
options.rationale: Wrong: Alternative splicing can affect membrane versus secreted forms but does not relocate VDJ to a different constant region; this would be correct only for membrane/secreted isoform changes.

question: During a prolonged infection, B cells in follicles acquire point mutations in antigen-binding regions. Which enzyme initiates these mutations?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: Activation induced cytidine deaminase introduces mutations in immunoglobulin genes
options.rationale: Correct: AID introduces point mutations in variable regions during somatic hypermutation, enabling affinity maturation as described in the lecture.

options.text: RAG recombinase mediates somatic hypermutation in germinal centers
options.rationale: Wrong: RAG enzymes mediate V(D)J recombination during development, not somatic hypermutation; it would be correct only if RAG acted post-activation, which it does not.

options.text: DNA polymerase delta error rate increases to mutate BCR variable regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation is initiated by AID, not general polymerase error; this would be correct only if polymerase errors were targeted specifically to variable regions.

options.text: Uracil DNA glycosylase directly creates point mutations in V regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Uracil DNA glycosylase participates in processing AID-induced lesions but AID is the initiating enzyme; this would be correct only if UDg initiated deamination itself.

options.text: Topoisomerase II generates double strand breaks to mutate antigen receptors
options.rationale: Wrong: Topoisomerase II is not the initiating mutator in somatic hypermutation; it would be correct only if it specifically targeted V regions to create mutations.

question: A patient with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections shows poor antibody affinity despite normal IgM levels. Which germinal center process is most likely defective?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: Selection of high affinity B cells by follicular dendritic cell displayed antigen
options.rationale: Correct: Affinity maturation requires FDC-displayed antigen and Tfh-mediated selection of high-affinity clones; defective selection explains poor affinity despite antibody presence.

options.text: Initial BCR cross-linking by repetitive polysaccharide antigens in spleen
options.rationale: Wrong: Initial BCR cross-linking can activate T-independent responses but does not produce affinity-matured antibodies; this would be correct only if activation itself were impaired.

options.text: Bone marrow V(D)J recombination failure producing nonfunctional naive BCRs
options.rationale: Wrong: V(D)J recombination defects affect naive repertoire and IgM levels; here IgM is normal, so this would be correct only if naive BCR generation were abnormal.

options.text: Complement receptor deficiency preventing classical pathway activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement defects can impair opsonization and antigen trapping but do not directly prevent affinity maturation; this would be correct only if complement were essential for FDC antigen display in this case.

options.text: Plasma cell inability to secrete any immunoglobulin despite normal B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: If plasma cells could not secrete antibodies, serum IgM would be low; normal IgM argues against a secretion defect, so this option is unlikely unless secretion were selectively impaired for high-affinity isotypes.

question: Which serum antibody pattern best distinguishes a primary response from a secondary response early after re-exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast a primary antibody response vs. a secondary antibody response.

options.text: Primary response shows early IgM predominance with low IgG initially
options.rationale: Correct: Primary responses produce IgM first with IgG rising later; the lecture notes IgM detected first and IgG:IgM ratio  2 early; this would be correct only if class switching and memory were absent.

options.text: Primary response shows sustained high IgG levels for prolonged periods
options.rationale: Wrong: Sustained high IgG is typical of secondary responses and long-lived plasma cells; this would be correct only after memory-driven re-exposure.

question: A vaccine aims to induce long-lived plasma cells and high-affinity antibodies. Which lymphoid microenvironment should the vaccine target to maximize these outcomes?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the phases of the humoral immune response and where each of these occurring and which cell types are involved.

options.text: Germinal center within secondary follicle where B cells specialize
options.rationale: Correct: Germinal centers in secondary follicles are where isotype switching, affinity maturation, and long-lived plasma cell generation occur, per the lecture.

options.text: Primary follicle containing resting B cells before antigen encounter
options.rationale: Wrong: Primary follicles contain resting B cells and lack the specialized processes of germinal centers; this would be correct only for naive B cell localization.

options.text: Paracortex where naive T cells are activated by antigen presenting cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Paracortex is T cell zone; while Tfh originate there, the B cell specialization occurs in follicles, so this would be correct only if T cell priming alone were sufficient.

options.text: Medullary sinus where macrophages filter lymph and trap debris
options.rationale: Wrong: Medullary sinuses are for filtration and plasma cell residence but not the primary site of affinity maturation; this would be correct only for terminal plasma cell localization.

options.text: Marginal zone of spleen specialized for T cell dependent germinal centers
options.rationale: Wrong: Marginal zone B cells mediate T-independent responses; germinal centers are not formed primarily in marginal zones, so this would be correct only in specific splenic follicle contexts.

question: Which receptor on phagocytes binds the Fc portion of IgG to enhance ingestion of opsonized microbes?
cited_learning_objective: Review: Describe the function of the FcRs discussed and the cells that express these receptors.

options.text: Fc gamma receptor CD64 on macrophages and neutrophils mediates opsonization
options.rationale: Correct: FcγR (CD64) on macrophages and neutrophils binds IgG Fc to promote phagocytosis, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Fc epsilon receptor on eosinophils binds IgG to promote phagocytosis
options.rationale: Wrong: FcεR binds IgE on eosinophils; it would be correct only if the question asked about IgE-mediated responses.

options.text: Complement receptor CR1 on neutrophils directly binds IgG Fc region
options.rationale: Wrong: CR1 binds complement fragments like C3b, not IgG Fc; this would be correct only if complement opsonization were the focus.

options.text: Fc alpha receptor on NK cells binds IgG to trigger ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: FcαR binds IgA and NK cells primarily use FcγR (CD16) for IgG-mediated ADCC; this would be correct only if IgA-mediated cytotoxicity by NK cells occurred.

options.text: Fc mu receptor on B cells binds IgG to enhance phagocytosis
options.rationale: Wrong: FcμR binds IgM and is expressed on B cells; it would be correct only if IgM-mediated phagocytosis by B cells were the mechanism.

question: A patient with high serum IgE and recurrent parasitic infections relies on which antibody-mediated effector cell interaction for parasite clearance?
cited_learning_objective: Review: Compare and contrast the effector functions of the various types of antibody isotypes.

options.text: Eosinophil Fc epsilon receptor engagement of IgE coated parasites mediates ADCC
options.rationale: Correct: IgE bound to parasites engages FcεR on eosinophils to mediate ADCC, as described in the lecture.

options.text: NK cell Fc gamma receptor engagement of IgM coated parasites mediates ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: NK cells use FcγR to bind IgG, not IgM; this would be correct only if parasites were coated with IgG instead of IgM.

options.text: Macrophage complement receptor binding of IgA immune complexes clears parasites
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement receptors bind complement fragments, and IgA is not the main complement activator; this would be correct only if IgA activated complement in that context.

options.text: Neutrophil Fc alpha receptor engagement of IgG triggers parasite phagocytosis
options.rationale: Wrong: FcαR binds IgA and neutrophils use FcγR for IgG; this would be correct only if IgA were the opsonin and FcαR mediated phagocytosis.

options.text: B cell Fc receptor binding of IgE directly lyses parasites extracellularly
options.rationale: Wrong: B cells do not mediate IgE-dependent cytotoxicity; this would be correct only if B cells expressed cytotoxic machinery and FcεR-mediated killing.

question: Which antibody isotype is most effective at activating the classical complement pathway when bound to multivalent antigen?
cited_learning_objective: Functions of the Humoral Immune Response

options.text: Pentameric IgM efficiently activates classical complement when antigen bound
options.rationale: Correct: IgM is highly effective at activating the classical complement pathway when bound to antigen due to its pentameric structure, per the lecture.

options.text: Monomeric IgA in mucosa robustly activates classical complement pathway
options.rationale: Wrong: IgA is not a strong activator of the classical pathway; this would be correct only if IgA could bind C1q effectively like IgM or IgG.

options.text: Secretory IgA in secretions primarily triggers systemic complement activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Secretory IgA functions mainly in mucosal neutralization and does not strongly activate systemic complement; this would be correct only if secretory IgA had complement-activating Fc regions.

options.text: IgE bound to helminths activates classical complement cascade efficiently
options.rationale: Wrong: IgE is not a primary activator of the classical complement pathway; this would be correct only if IgE could bind C1q similarly to IgM.

options.text: IgG subclasses never participate in classical complement activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Some IgG subclasses (e.g., IgG1, IgG3) can activate complement; this option would be correct only if all IgG subclasses lacked C1q binding.

question: Which two signals are required for full activation of a naive follicular B cell encountering protein antigen?
cited_learning_objective: Phases of Humoral Immunity

options.text: BCR engagement plus TLR or complement receptor costimulatory signals
options.rationale: Correct: First signal is BCR binding; second signals include innate inputs like complement receptor CD21 or TLRs, as described in activation steps.

options.text: Only BCR cross-linking without any additional costimulatory input
options.rationale: Wrong: Some B cells (B-1, marginal-zone) can be activated by cross-linking alone, but follicular B cells typically require a second signal; this would be correct only for T-independent subsets.

options.text: CD8 T cell cytotoxic contact plus BCR internalization signal
options.rationale: Wrong: CD8 T cells do not provide helper signals for B cells; this would be correct only if cytotoxic T cells expressed CD40L and provided help, which they do not.

options.text: Complement activation alone without BCR engagement suffices for activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement can provide costimulation but cannot replace antigen-specific BCR engagement; this would be correct only if complement triggered BCR-independent activation pathways.

options.text: FDC antigen presentation alone without BCR recognition activates B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: FDCs display antigen for BCR recognition but cannot activate B cells without BCR engagement; this would be correct only if B cells could be activated solely by FDC signals.

question: A researcher blocks CD40:CD40L interactions during an immune response. Which germinal center outcome will be most reduced?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: ii. Isotype Switching

options.text: Affinity maturation and class switching will be markedly decreased without CD40L
options.rationale: Correct: CD40:CD40L engagement is required for AID activation, isotype switching, and affinity maturation in germinal centers, per the lecture.

options.text: Initial antigen recognition by naive B cells will be completely abolished
options.rationale: Wrong: Initial antigen recognition via BCR does not require CD40:CD40L; this would be correct only if BCR signaling components were inhibited.

options.text: FDC ability to trap antigen on their surface will be eliminated
options.rationale: Wrong: FDC antigen trapping is independent of CD40:CD40L; this would be correct only if CD40 signaling controlled FDC antigen retention.

options.text: T cell priming in paracortex will be enhanced by blocking CD40L
options.rationale: Wrong: Blocking CD40L impairs T-B interactions rather than enhancing T cell priming; this would be correct only if CD40L blockade paradoxically increased T cell activation.

options.text: Somatic hypermutation frequency will increase without CD40 signaling
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation requires AID activation via T cell help; CD40L blockade would reduce, not increase, mutation frequency unless alternative AID activation occurred.

question: Which B cell-derived product neutralizes toxins and prevents pathogen entry into host cells in the extracellular space?
cited_learning_objective: Functions of the Humoral Immune Response

options.text: Antibody is secreted by plasma cells to neutralize microbes and toxins
options.rationale: Correct: Secreted antibodies neutralize microbes, viruses, and toxins in extracellular spaces, as stated in the lecture functions.

options.text: Complement proteins produced by B cells directly neutralize extracellular pathogens
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement proteins are produced mainly by the liver, not B cells; this would be correct only if B cells secreted complement components.

options.text: Cytokines from plasma cells recruit neutrophils to neutralize toxins
options.rationale: Wrong: Plasma cells primarily secrete antibodies, not cytokines for neutrophil recruitment; this would be correct only if plasma cells secreted those specific chemokines.

options.text: Membrane-bound BCRs on naive B cells neutralize extracellular toxins
options.rationale: Wrong: Membrane BCRs bind antigen for activation but do not neutralize toxins extracellularly; this would be correct only if BCRs were shed as neutralizing molecules.

options.text: Fc receptors on macrophages neutralize pathogens before antibody binding
options.rationale: Wrong: Fc receptors bind antibody-opsonized targets and mediate phagocytosis, but they do not neutralize pathogens independently; this would be correct only if FcRs acted without antibodies.

question: A patient with defective AID activity would most likely show which laboratory finding after immunization with a protein antigen?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: High IgM titers with low affinity and minimal class switched IgG
options.rationale: Correct: AID is required for somatic hypermutation and class switching; deficiency yields persistent IgM with poor affinity and reduced IgG, matching lecture mechanisms.

options.text: High affinity IgG with normal class switching and memory formation
options.rationale: Wrong: AID deficiency prevents affinity maturation and class switching; this would be correct only if AID function were intact.

options.text: Absent IgM but abundant high affinity IgA in serum
options.rationale: Wrong: AID deficiency would not produce abundant class-switched isotypes like IgA; this would be correct only if alternative switching pathways compensated fully.

options.text: Excessive germinal center formation with hypermutated variable regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Without AID, somatic hypermutation and effective germinal center selection are impaired; this would be correct only if hypermutation occurred via another enzyme.

options.text: Normal secondary response kinetics with rapid IgG rise after boost
options.rationale: Wrong: AID deficiency impairs secondary high-affinity IgG responses; this would be correct only if memory B cells and switching were unaffected.

question: Which cell type displays antigen on Fc or complement receptors to facilitate selection of high affinity B cells in follicles?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: Follicular dendritic cells trap antigen for B cell selection in germinal centers
options.rationale: Correct: FDCs display antigen via Fc or complement receptors to activated B cells, enabling selection of high-affinity clones as described in the lecture.

options.text: Conventional dendritic cells present antigen via MHC I to B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Conventional DCs present to T cells via MHC, not to B cells via Fc/complement receptors; this would be correct only if DCs displayed antigen in FDC-like fashion.

options.text: Macrophages present antigen on MHC II to select high affinity B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Macrophages present antigen to T cells and clear debris but FDCs specifically display intact antigen to B cells; this would be correct only if macrophages acted like FDCs.

options.text: T follicular helper cells present intact antigen on surface to B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Tfh cells provide help via CD40L and cytokines and recognize processed peptide-MHC II, not display intact antigen via Fc/complement receptors; this would be correct only if Tfh displayed antigen similarly to FDCs.

options.text: Naive B cells themselves display antigen to neighboring B cells for selection
options.rationale: Wrong: Naive B cells internalize and present processed antigen to T cells but do not trap intact antigen for selection; this would be correct only if B cells functioned as antigen-retaining stromal cells.

question: A child vaccinated with a polysaccharide capsule conjugate vaccine develops robust IgG and memory. Which mechanism explains improved response compared with unconjugated polysaccharide vaccine?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast T-dependent vs. T-independent antibody responses and the different subsets of B cells.

options.text: Protein conjugation enables peptide presentation to helper T cells and class switching
options.rationale: Correct: Conjugating polysaccharide to protein allows B cells to present peptide to Tfh cells, enabling T-dependent isotype switching and memory formation, per lecture contrasts.

options.text: Conjugation increases polysaccharide cross-linking of BCRs for T independent activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Cross-linking drives T-independent responses but does not explain enhanced IgG and memory; this would be correct only if conjugation increased repetitive epitope density without T cell help.

options.text: Conjugate vaccines directly activate complement to produce IgG without T cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement activation alone does not generate class-switched IgG and memory; this would be correct only if complement induced T-dependent features.

options.text: Protein carrier prevents antigen uptake by follicular dendritic cells limiting response
options.rationale: Wrong: Carrier proteins enhance antigen presentation and FDC display rather than preventing uptake; this would be correct only if carrier blocked FDC antigen retention.

options.text: Conjugation converts marginal-zone B cell responses into bone marrow plasma cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Marginal-zone B cells mediate T-independent responses; conjugation promotes follicular B cell T-dependent responses and memory, not direct marginal-zone conversion.

question: Which statement best describes the fate of B cells that acquire lower affinity BCRs during germinal center competition?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: Lower affinity B cells undergo apoptosis due to lack of Tfh survival signals
options.rationale: Correct: B cells with lower affinity fail to compete for antigen and Tfh help and die by neglect, as outlined in the lecture.

options.text: Lower affinity B cells are preferentially selected to become long lived plasma cells
options.rationale: Wrong: High affinity clones are preferentially selected for plasma cell differentiation; this would be correct only if selection favored diversity over affinity.

options.text: Lower affinity B cells switch isotype to IgE to increase binding strength
options.rationale: Wrong: Isotype switching changes Fc function, not antigen-binding affinity; this would be correct only if switching directly increased variable region affinity.

options.text: Lower affinity B cells migrate to paracortex to present antigen to naive T cells
options.rationale: Wrong: B cells present antigen to Tfh in follicles; migration to paracortex is not the typical fate for low-affinity clones unless they re-enter T cell zones for other interactions.

options.text: Lower affinity B cells upregulate AID to rapidly increase mutation rate
options.rationale: Wrong: AID activity is present in germinal centers but upregulation alone does not guarantee survival; this would be correct only if increased mutation reliably produced higher affinity variants.

question: Which immunoglobulin isotype predominates early in a primary humoral response and is produced by naive B cells before class switching?
cited_learning_objective: Phases of Humoral Immunity

options.text: IgM is produced first by naive B cells before isotype switching occurs
options.rationale: Correct: Naive B cells initially secrete IgM upon activation; class switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE occurs later with T cell help, as the lecture states.

options.text: IgG is the earliest isotype produced immediately by naive B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: IgG production requires class switching and T cell help; this would be correct only in a secondary response with memory B cells.

options.text: IgA predominates early in systemic primary responses before switching
options.rationale: Wrong: IgA is typically produced after class switching, especially at mucosal sites; this would be correct only if mucosal switching occurred immediately.

options.text: IgE is secreted first in primary responses to most protein antigens
options.rationale: Wrong: IgE arises after class switching influenced by cytokines like IL-4; this would be correct only in allergic-type responses with appropriate cytokine milieu.

options.text: Secretory IgA from plasma cells is the initial systemic antibody produced
options.rationale: Wrong: Secretory IgA is a mucosal antibody and not the initial systemic antibody; this would be correct only for mucosal primary exposures with rapid class switching.

question: A patient with defective CD21 (complement receptor) on B cells shows impaired responses to microbes. Which activation step is directly affected?
cited_learning_objective: Phases of Humoral Immunity

options.text: Second signal amplification via complement receptor costimulation will be reduced
options.rationale: Correct: CD21 (complement receptor) provides a second signal enhancing B cell activation; its deficiency reduces costimulatory signaling as noted in activation steps.

options.text: Primary antigen recognition by BCR will be completely abolished without CD21
options.rationale: Wrong: BCR antigen recognition is independent of CD21; this would be correct only if BCR expression or function were lost.

options.text: Tfh cell cytokine secretion will be increased to compensate for CD21 loss
options.rationale: Wrong: CD21 deficiency does not inherently increase Tfh cytokines; this would be correct only if compensatory T cell responses were experimentally induced.

options.text: Somatic hypermutation will proceed normally without any impact
options.rationale: Wrong: While somatic hypermutation requires AID and Tfh help, CD21-mediated antigen trapping can influence germinal center reactions; this would be correct only if alternative antigen presentation fully compensated.

options.text: Complement classical pathway activation by IgM will be enhanced by CD21 loss
options.rationale: Wrong: CD21 loss does not enhance complement activation; this would be correct only if CD21 normally inhibited complement, which it does not.

question: Which helper T cell subset predominantly provides the signals (CD40L and cytokines) that drive germinal center B cell proliferation and differentiation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how CD4 T cells "help" B cells. Identify the predominant Th subset involved in the humoral response.

options.text: T follicular helper cells provide CD40L and cytokines to support B cells
options.rationale: Correct: Tfh cells migrate into follicles and provide CD40L and cytokines that promote isotype switching, affinity maturation, and plasma cell differentiation, per the lecture.

options.text: Th17 cells primarily provide CD40L signals for germinal center reactions
options.rationale: Wrong: Th17 cells are not the main providers of CD40L in germinal centers; this would be correct only if Th17 cells adopted Tfh functions.

options.text: Regulatory T cells enhance B cell proliferation via CD40L expression
options.rationale: Wrong: Tregs suppress immune responses and do not typically provide CD40L help; this would be correct only if Tregs were reprogrammed to helper phenotype.

options.text: Cytotoxic CD8 T cells supply cytokines and CD40L to B cells in follicles
options.rationale: Wrong: CD8 T cells do not normally provide CD40L-mediated help to B cells; this would be correct only in an unusual experimental context.

options.text: Naive CD4 T cells in paracortex directly drive germinal center B cell selection
options.rationale: Wrong: Naive CD4 T cells must differentiate into Tfh to assist germinal center B cells; this would be correct only if naive cells immediately expressed Tfh markers.

question: Which outcome is expected when B cells present processed peptide on MHC II to activated CD4 T cells at the T–B border?
cited_learning_objective: T Helper Cells and their Role in Humoral Responses

options.text: Initial extrafollicular plasmablast generation with low affinity antibody production
options.rationale: Correct: Early T–B interactions at extrafollicular foci produce short-lived plasma cells and lower affinity antibodies before germinal center formation, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Immediate formation of long lived plasma cells and high affinity IgG production
options.rationale: Wrong: Long-lived plasma cells and high-affinity IgG arise mainly from germinal center reactions, not initial extrafollicular interactions; this would be correct only after GC maturation.

options.text: Suppression of B cell proliferation and prevention of isotype switching
options.rationale: Wrong: T–B cognate interactions promote proliferation and switching; suppression would occur only if regulatory signals dominated the interaction.

options.text: Activation of CD8 T cells to mediate antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity
options.rationale: Wrong: CD4 T cell help to B cells does not directly activate CD8-mediated ADCC; this would be correct only if cross-priming to CD8 occurred concurrently.

options.text: Immediate migration of B cells to bone marrow to become plasma cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Some plasmablasts may migrate, but long-lived bone marrow plasma cells are typically generated after germinal center maturation; this would be correct only for a subset of early plasmablasts.

question: Which feature distinguishes T-independent antigens from T-dependent antigens in terms of B cell activation requirements?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast T-dependent vs. T-independent antibody responses and the different subsets of B cells.

options.text: T independent antigens cross link many BCRs and do not need T cell help
options.rationale: Correct: T-independent antigens are repetitive and can cross-link BCRs to activate B-1 or marginal-zone B cells without T cell help, as the lecture explains.

options.text: T dependent antigens are nonprotein repetitive epitopes activating B cells alone
options.rationale: Wrong: T-dependent antigens are typically proteins requiring T cell help; this would be correct only if nonprotein antigens required T cells, which they generally do not.

options.text: T independent responses generate robust affinity maturation and memory B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: T-independent responses show little affinity maturation and poor memory; this would be correct only if T-independent pathways supported germinal center reactions.

options.text: T dependent antigens never undergo isotype switching to IgG or IgA
options.rationale: Wrong: T-dependent responses commonly undergo isotype switching; this would be correct only if class switching were impossible in T-dependent contexts.

options.text: T independent antigens always require complement receptor engagement for activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement can provide a second signal but is not always required for T-independent activation; this would be correct only if complement were universally necessary.

question: Which experimental finding would best indicate successful affinity maturation after repeated antigen exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: Serum antibodies show increased binding strength and somatic mutations in V regions
options.rationale: Correct: Affinity maturation is characterized by somatic hypermutation in variable regions and selection of higher-affinity antibodies, leading to increased binding strength.

options.text: Serum IgM levels rise while IgG remains undetectable after boosting
options.rationale: Wrong: Boosting typically increases class-switched IgG with higher affinity; this would be correct only if class switching failed.

options.text: Germinal centers disappear and no B cell proliferation is observed
options.rationale: Wrong: Affinity maturation occurs within active germinal centers; disappearance of GCs would indicate lack of maturation, not success.

options.text: Fewer somatic mutations in variable regions with broader low affinity binding
options.rationale: Wrong: Successful affinity maturation yields more, not fewer, beneficial mutations and narrower higher-affinity specificity; this would be correct only if selection favored breadth over affinity.

options.text: Increased IgE titers without changes in variable region sequences
options.rationale: Wrong: IgE increase does not equate to affinity maturation; this would be correct only if isotype switching to IgE coincided with hypermutation, which is not the primary marker.

question: A patient with splenectomy is particularly susceptible to encapsulated bacteria. Which B cell compartment normally contributes to early responses against such organisms?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast T-dependent vs. T-independent antibody responses and the different subsets of B cells.

options.text: Marginal-zone B cells at splenic white pulp border mediate early responses
options.rationale: Correct: Marginal-zone B cells in the spleen respond rapidly to blood-borne encapsulated bacteria, providing T-independent responses as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Follicular B cells in lymph node cortex mediate immediate splenic defense
options.rationale: Wrong: Follicular B cells are T-dependent and circulate through lymphoid tissues; this would be correct only if follicular B cells were the primary splenic responders.

options.text: Bone marrow plasma cells provide the first line defense against encapsulated bacteria
options.rationale: Wrong: Bone marrow plasma cells are long-lived antibody producers but not the immediate responders to new blood-borne encapsulated bacteria; this would be correct only if preexisting antibodies were present.

options.text: B-1 cells in thymus produce high affinity IgG against capsules rapidly
options.rationale: Wrong: B-1 cells are in peritoneum and mucosa and produce natural antibodies, not necessarily high-affinity IgG; this would be correct only if B-1 cells produced class-switched high-affinity IgG.

options.text: T follicular helper cells in spleen directly phagocytose encapsulated organisms
options.rationale: Wrong: Tfh cells provide help to B cells but do not phagocytose bacteria; this would be correct only if Tfh had phagocytic function.

question: Which laboratory ratio would you expect early in a symptomatic primary infection according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Primary vs. Secondary Humoral Responses: Serum Levels of IgM vs. IgG

options.text: IgG to IgM ratio less than one during early symptomatic primary infection
options.rationale: Correct: In primary responses IgM appears first and IgG:IgM ratio is  2 is characteristic of secondary responses; this would be correct only after re-exposure with memory B cells.

options.text: IgM absent with only IgG detectable in early primary infection
options.rationale: Wrong: IgM is typically present early in primary infection; this would be correct only if IgM production were selectively impaired.

options.text: Equal IgG and IgM levels with ratio exactly one during early infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Early primary infection usually shows IgM predominance; equality would be correct only at a transitional time point later in the response.

options.text: IgA predominance in serum with negligible IgM during primary systemic infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Serum IgA is not typically predominant in systemic primary infections; this would be correct only for mucosal exposures with rapid IgA switching.

question: Which mechanism explains why secondary humoral responses produce higher antibody titers more rapidly than primary responses?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast a primary antibody response vs. a secondary antibody response.

options.text: Memory B cells rapidly expand and produce class switched high affinity antibodies
options.rationale: Correct: Memory B cells generated after primary exposure respond quickly upon re-exposure, producing high-titer, class-switched, affinity-matured antibodies as described in the lecture.

options.text: Naive B cells undergo faster V(D)J recombination during secondary exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: V(D)J recombination occurs during development, not during secondary responses; this would be correct only if naive recombination accelerated upon re-exposure.

options.text: Complement activation alone drives rapid IgG production without B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement does not replace B cell memory; rapid IgG production requires memory B cells, so this would be correct only if complement induced class switching directly.

options.text: T independent B cell subsets convert to memory B cells after first exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: T-independent responses generate little memory; this would be correct only if T-independent pathways produced robust memory formation.

options.text: FDCs alone secrete antibodies rapidly upon antigen reappearance
options.rationale: Wrong: FDCs display antigen but do not secrete antibodies; this would be correct only if FDCs had antibody-secreting capacity.

question: Which Fc receptor is primarily used by NK cells to mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity against IgG-coated targets?
cited_learning_objective: Functions of the Humoral Immune Response

options.text: Fc gamma receptor CD16 on NK cells binds IgG to trigger ADCC
options.rationale: Correct: NK cells express FcγRIII (CD16) which binds IgG-coated targets to mediate ADCC, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Fc epsilon receptor on NK cells binds IgG to mediate ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: FcεR binds IgE and is expressed on eosinophils and mast cells, not NK cells; this would be correct only if NK cells expressed FcεR and IgE mediated ADCC.

options.text: Fc alpha receptor on NK cells binds IgM to induce cytotoxicity
options.rationale: Wrong: FcαR binds IgA and NK cells primarily use FcγR for IgG; this would be correct only if NK cells used FcαR for IgM, which is incorrect.

options.text: Complement receptor CR3 on NK cells binds IgG to trigger ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: CR3 binds complement fragments, not IgG Fc; this would be correct only if complement mediated NK activation directly.

options.text: Fc mu receptor on NK cells binds IgM to mediate ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: FcμR binds IgM and is not the primary mediator of NK cell ADCC; this would be correct only if NK cells used FcμR for cytotoxicity.

question: Which process explains how a B cell maintains antigen specificity while changing effector function of its antibody?
cited_learning_objective: Isotype Switching: Switching from IgM to IgA, IgG, or IgE

options.text: Switch recombination replaces heavy chain constant region while preserving VDJ specificity
options.rationale: Correct: Class switch recombination excises intervening constant region DNA, moving the same VDJ cassette to a new constant region, preserving antigen specificity while changing Fc function.

options.text: Somatic hypermutation alters constant region to change effector functions
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation targets variable regions for affinity changes, not constant regions; this would be correct only if constant regions were mutated to alter Fc.

options.text: Alternative V(D)J recombination swaps variable regions between B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: V(D)J recombination occurs during development and does not swap V regions between mature B cells; this would be correct only in engineered experimental systems.

options.text: Proteolytic cleavage of IgM Fc converts it into IgG functional form
options.rationale: Wrong: Proteolysis does not convert isotypes; class switching is a genomic recombination event, so this would be correct only if proteolysis changed constant region identity.

options.text: Somatic recombination of light chain constant region changes isotype
options.rationale: Wrong: Isotype switching involves heavy chain constant regions, not light chain constant regions; this would be correct only if light chain constants determined isotype.

question: Which experimental manipulation would most directly prevent both isotype switching and somatic hypermutation in activated B cells?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation; ii. Isotype Switching

options.text: Genetic deletion of activation induced cytidine deaminase abolishes both processes
options.rationale: Correct: AID is required for both somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination; deleting AID prevents these germinal center processes as the lecture explains.

options.text: Blocking CD21 complement receptor on B cells prevents AID expression directly
options.rationale: Wrong: CD21 provides costimulation but does not directly induce AID; this would be correct only if CD21 signaling were the sole AID inducer.

options.text: Inhibiting RAG recombinase during activation blocks somatic hypermutation
options.rationale: Wrong: RAG mediates V(D)J recombination during development, not somatic hypermutation; this would be correct only if RAG were repurposed in germinal centers.

options.text: Neutralizing complement C3 prevents point mutations in variable regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement influences antigen trapping but AID initiates mutations; this would be correct only if complement were essential for AID activation.

options.text: Deleting CD8 T cells eliminates class switching and hypermutation in B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: CD8 T cells are not the helper subset for B cells; this would be correct only if CD8 cells provided CD40L and cytokines in vivo.

question: Which description best captures the role of follicular dendritic cells in germinal centers?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the process in detail and biological significance of: i. Affinity Maturation

options.text: FDCs retain intact antigen via Fc and complement receptors for B cell selection
options.rationale: Correct: FDCs trap and display intact antigen using Fc and complement receptors to enable selection of high-affinity B cells, as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: FDCs present processed peptide on MHC II to activate naive CD8 T cells
options.rationale: Wrong: FDCs do not present antigen on MHC II to T cells; they display intact antigen to B cells, so this would be correct only if FDCs functioned as classical APCs.

options.text: FDCs secrete antibodies to neutralize pathogens within germinal centers
options.rationale: Wrong: FDCs are stromal cells that trap antigen but do not secrete antibodies; this would be correct only if FDCs had plasma cell functions.

options.text: FDCs are bone marrow derived macrophages clearing apoptotic B cells
options.rationale: Wrong: FDCs are stromal and not bone marrow-derived macrophages; this would be correct only if FDCs originated from hematopoietic lineage.

options.text: FDCs provide CD40L signals to drive B cell isotype switching directly
options.rationale: Wrong: CD40L is provided by Tfh cells, not FDCs; this would be correct only if FDCs expressed CD40L and functioned as T cell surrogates.

question: Which clinical strategy leverages T-dependent mechanisms to improve immunogenicity of a polysaccharide antigen in infants?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast T-dependent vs. T-independent antibody responses and the different subsets of B cells.

options.text: Conjugating polysaccharide to protein carrier to recruit helper T cell responses
options.rationale: Correct: Conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharides into T-dependent antigens by providing peptide for T cell help, enabling class switching and memory as discussed in the lecture.

options.text: Administering polysaccharide alone to maximize BCR cross linking in infants
options.rationale: Wrong: Polysaccharide alone elicits weak responses in infants due to immature T-independent responses; this would be correct only if infants had mature marginal-zone B cell function.

options.text: Using high dose polysaccharide to induce somatic hypermutation without T cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Somatic hypermutation requires AID and Tfh help; high antigen dose alone does not substitute for T-dependent mechanisms, so this would be correct only in an artificial system.

options.text: Co-administering complement inhibitors to enhance B cell activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement provides costimulatory signals; inhibiting complement would reduce, not enhance, B cell activation, so this would be correct only if complement were suppressive.

options.text: Delivering antigen directly into bone marrow to stimulate plasma cell niches
options.rationale: Wrong: Bone marrow plasma cell niches support long-lived cells but do not replace the need for T-dependent germinal center reactions in infants; this would be correct only if bone marrow delivery induced Tfh-independent memory.

question: Which observation would indicate a predominantly T-independent antibody response after exposure to a bacterial polysaccharide?
cited_learning_objective: Two Major Types of Antibody Responses: T-Dependent and T-independent

options.text: Predominant IgM production with minimal affinity maturation and poor memory formation
options.rationale: Correct: T-independent responses typically yield mainly IgM, little affinity maturation, and poor memory, matching the lecture description.

options.text: Rapid high affinity IgG response with robust memory B cell generation
options.rationale: Wrong: Rapid high-affinity IgG and memory are hallmarks of T-dependent responses; this would be correct only if T cell help were present.

options.text: Extensive germinal center formation with class switching to IgA
options.rationale: Wrong: Germinal centers and class switching are features of T-dependent responses; this would be correct only if Tfh-mediated GC reactions occurred.

options.text: Sustained high IgG titers with IgG to IgM ratio greater than two early
options.rationale: Wrong: Early IgG predominance (IgG:IgM >2) indicates secondary or T-dependent responses; this would be correct only after memory formation.

options.text: Exclusive production of IgE antibodies with eosinophil mediated ADCC
options.rationale: Wrong: IgE production is typically T-dependent and associated with Th2 cytokines; this would be correct only in allergic or helminth contexts with T cell help.

question: Which experimental evidence would directly demonstrate that CD40 engagement activates AID in B cells?
cited_learning_objective: Isotype Switching: Switching from IgM to IgA, IgG, or IgE

options.text: In vitro CD40 stimulation increases AID mRNA and induces class switch recombination
options.rationale: Correct: CD40 engagement activates AID expression leading to switch recombination; observing increased AID transcripts and switching after CD40 stimulation directly supports this mechanism.

options.text: Blocking CD40 increases somatic hypermutation frequency in variable regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Blocking CD40 would reduce AID activity and hypermutation; this would be correct only if CD40 blockade paradoxically activated alternative mutational pathways.

options.text: CD40 stimulation alone causes immediate secretion of high affinity IgG without AID
options.rationale: Wrong: High-affinity IgG secretion requires AID-mediated hypermutation and switching; this would be correct only if AID were unnecessary for class switching.

options.text: AID expression is constitutive in naive B cells independent of CD40 signals
options.rationale: Wrong: AID is induced upon activation and CD40 engagement; constitutive expression would be correct only if AID were always active in naive cells.

options.text: CD40 engagement prevents DNA breaks in switch regions and reduces recombination
options.rationale: Wrong: CD40 engagement promotes AID activity and DNA breaks in switch regions; this would be correct only if CD40 signaling inhibited AID-induced breaks.

question: Which statement best explains why marginal-zone and B-1 B cells produce 'natural antibodies' that clear apoptotic cells and debris?
cited_learning_objective: Two Major Types of Antibody Responses: T-Dependent and T-independent

options.text: These innate-like B cells produce low affinity broad specificity IgM without T help
options.rationale: Correct: B-1 and marginal-zone B cells produce natural IgM with broad specificity to clear debris and apoptotic cells without T cell help, as the lecture notes.

options.text: They undergo extensive affinity maturation to generate high specificity antibodies
options.rationale: Wrong: Natural antibodies are typically low affinity and germline-encoded; this would be correct only if these cells underwent germinal center hypermutation.

options.text: They require Tfh cell interactions to secrete natural IgM constitutively
options.rationale: Wrong: Natural antibody production by B-1 cells is largely T-independent; this would be correct only if Tfh were necessary for baseline secretion.

options.text: They primarily secrete class-switched IgG for apoptotic cell clearance
options.rationale: Wrong: Natural antibodies are mainly IgM; this would be correct only if class switching occurred constitutively in these subsets.

options.text: They express high levels of AID to constantly mutate variable regions
options.rationale: Wrong: Constant AID expression would lead to hypermutation, not characteristic of natural antibody producers; this would be correct only in pathological conditions.

question: Which clinical intervention would most directly enhance opsonization of bacteria for macrophage phagocytosis?
cited_learning_objective: Functions of the Humoral Immune Response

options.text: Administering pathogen specific IgG to increase Fc mediated opsonization
options.rationale: Correct: Providing specific IgG increases Fc-mediated opsonization via Fcγ receptors on macrophages, enhancing phagocytosis as described in the lecture.

options.text: Giving intravenous IgM to directly activate macrophage Fc receptors
options.rationale: Wrong: Macrophage Fc receptors primarily bind IgG; IV IgM does not directly engage FcγR to enhance phagocytosis, so this would be correct only if macrophages used FcμR for opsonization.

options.text: Blocking complement to prevent immune complex deposition and improve phagocytosis
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement enhances opsonization; blocking it would reduce phagocytosis, so this would be correct only if complement-mediated pathology impeded clearance.

options.text: Administering anti IgE antibodies to increase neutrophil mediated ingestion
options.rationale: Wrong: Anti-IgE reduces IgE-mediated responses and would not enhance macrophage opsonization by IgG; this would be correct only in IgE-driven pathology.

options.text: Infusing Tfh cells to directly phagocytose bacteria in bloodstream
options.rationale: Wrong: Tfh cells provide B cell help but do not phagocytose bacteria; this would be correct only if Tfh had acquired phagocytic function.

question: Which pattern of antibody isotype switching would you expect if a B cell receives IL-4 dominated cytokine signals from helper T cells?
cited_learning_objective: T Helper Cells and their Role in Humoral Responses

options.text: Switching toward IgE and certain IgG subclasses promoted by IL-4 signals
options.rationale: Correct: IL-4 from helper T cells guides isotype switching toward IgE and some IgG subclasses, consistent with cytokine-directed switching described in the lecture.

options.text: Switching exclusively to IgA in systemic compartments driven by IL-4
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-4 favors IgE and some IgG, not exclusively IgA; IgA switching is more associated with mucosal cytokines like TGF-β, so this would be correct only with different cytokine milieu.

options.text: IL-4 prevents any class switching and maintains IgM secretion indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-4 promotes switching rather than preventing it; this would be correct only if IL-4 inhibited AID, which it does not.

options.text: IL-4 drives somatic hypermutation but blocks isotype switching entirely
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-4 influences isotype switching and can support germinal center reactions; blocking switching while promoting hypermutation would be inconsistent with known cytokine roles.

options.text: IL-4 converts marginal-zone B cells into Tfh cells producing cytokines
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-4 does not transdifferentiate B cells into Tfh cells; this would be correct only in an artificial experimental reprogramming scenario.

question: Which laboratory finding would best indicate a successful secondary humoral response within days of re-exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Primary vs. Secondary Humoral Responses: Serum Levels of IgM vs. IgG

options.text: Rapid high serum IgG levels with IgG to IgM ratio greater than two early
options.rationale: Correct: Secondary responses produce rapid, high IgG titers and an IgG:IgM ratio >2 early, reflecting memory B cell activation as the lecture states.

options.text: Delayed IgG rise with prolonged IgM predominance over weeks
options.rationale: Wrong: Delayed IgG and prolonged IgM characterize primary responses; this would be correct only if memory formation failed.

options.text: Exclusive IgA response in serum without any IgG or IgM increase
options.rationale: Wrong: Secondary systemic responses typically involve IgG; exclusive IgA would be correct only for mucosal re-exposure with localized switching.

options.text: No antibody increase due to immediate complement mediated clearance
options.rationale: Wrong: Complement clearance does not prevent memory B cell activation and antibody production; this would be correct only if antigen were removed before B cell recognition.

options.text: Gradual low titer IgG increase over several months after re-exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: Secondary responses are rapid and high-titer; gradual low titer increase would be correct only in immunocompromised individuals with impaired memory responses.
